lessons.title: A Christmas Carol: context
lessons.summary: Explore the Victorian world Dickens was writing in, from workhouses and the Poor Law to the revival of Christmas, and learn how to weave context into an exam answer for AO3.
objectives: I can describe the key social conditions of 1840s Britain that shaped A Christmas Carol.
I can explain how Dickens's own experiences and beliefs influenced the novella.
I can link specific moments in the text to their historical and social context.
I can use context to deepen analysis rather than adding it as a separate fact.

activities.title: Britain in 1843: a divided nation
activities.content:
## Britain in 1843

Dickens wrote *A Christmas Carol* in just six weeks in the autumn of 1843. It was published on 19 December and sold out by Christmas Eve. To understand why it struck such a chord, you need to picture the country it appeared in.

**The Industrial Revolution** had transformed Britain. Factories, mills and railways created enormous wealth, and a new **middle class** of business owners, bankers and clerks grew rich. Scrooge belongs to this world: he is a money-lender in the City of London.

But the same changes pulled hundreds of thousands of people into overcrowded cities. In London, poor families lived in damp cellars and crowded courts, often several to a room. Disease spread quickly, child mortality was high, and wages in many trades were barely enough to survive on.

The 1840s became known as the **Hungry Forties**. Poor harvests, high bread prices and unemployment meant that hunger was a daily reality for many. Dickens walked London's streets at night and saw this for himself. His novella is not a fairy tale set in a vague past: it is a direct response to a real crisis, aimed at readers who had the power to do something about it.

activities.title: Linking context to a moment in the text
activities.content:
**How does context help us read the charity collectors' scene in Stave One?**

When the two gentlemen ask Scrooge for a donation, he replies: *"Are there no prisons?"* and *"And the Union workhouses? Are they still in operation?"*

| What the text says | What a Victorian reader would know | What this adds to our reading |
|---|---|---|
| Scrooge mentions prisons and workhouses | These were the harsh official 'solutions' to poverty under the 1834 Poor Law | Scrooge is not inventing cruelty; he is repeating the standard attitude of many wealthy people |
| He calls them "still in operation" | Workhouses were deliberately made unpleasant to discourage people from entering | He treats institutions designed to punish the poor as perfectly adequate |

Notice the pattern: **text → context → deeper meaning**. Dickens uses Scrooge as a mouthpiece for real opinions of the time, so that when Scrooge changes, the reader is invited to change too.

question.text: Why was the decade in which *A Christmas Carol* was published known as the 'Hungry Forties'?
question.hint: Think about food prices and work, not about Christmas dinners.
question.explanation: Poor harvests, high bread prices and unemployment made hunger a daily reality for many working people in the 1840s. Dickens wrote the novella against this background.

options.text: Poor harvests, high food prices and unemployment left many people hungry
Christmas feasts had become so large that people ate very little for the rest of the year
options.feedback: Most poor families could not afford a Christmas feast at all.

options.text: Britain was at war and food was rationed
options.feedback: Rationing belongs to the twentieth century, not the 1840s.

options.text: Factory owners refused to let workers eat during their shifts

activities.title: The Poor Law, workhouses and 'surplus population'
activities.content:
## The 1834 Poor Law

Before 1834, parishes gave small amounts of money or food to poor families in their own homes. Many wealthy people thought this encouraged laziness. The **Poor Law Amendment Act 1834** changed the system: help was now only available inside a **workhouse**.

Workhouses were designed to be worse than the lowest-paid job outside, so that only the truly desperate would enter. Families were split up, food was meagre, and inmates did hard, repetitive work such as breaking stones or picking apart old rope. Many poor people said they would rather die than go in.

## Malthus and the 'surplus population'

The economist **Thomas Malthus** had argued that population grows faster than food supply, so poverty and famine were natural checks on numbers. Some wealthy Victorians used this idea to excuse doing nothing: if the poor died, that simply reduced the 'surplus'.

Scrooge echoes this almost word for word when he says the poor had better die and *"decrease the surplus population."* Later, the Ghost of Christmas Present throws the phrase back at him when Scrooge asks whether Tiny Tim will live. The moment is painful because Scrooge now has a face and a name for the 'surplus' he dismissed so easily. Dickens is attacking a whole way of thinking, not just one mean old man.

activities.title: A model paragraph using context (AO3)
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Dickens present attitudes to the poor in *A Christmas Carol*?

> Dickens presents Scrooge's attitude to the poor as cold and theoretical. When told that many would rather die than enter a workhouse, Scrooge replies that they had better do it and "decrease the surplus population." The phrase comes directly from Malthusian economics, which was used by some Victorians to justify leaving the poor to starve. By placing this argument in the mouth of his miser, Dickens exposes it as heartless. The Ghost of Christmas Present later repeats Scrooge's own words when he asks about Tiny Tim, forcing Scrooge, and the reader, to see that 'surplus population' means real children. The context of the 1834 Poor Law, which made relief deliberately harsh, helps explain why Dickens felt such urgency: he wanted his middle-class readers to reject these attitudes before it was too late.

**Why this works:**
- Context is **tied to a quotation**, not dumped at the start.
- It explains **why Dickens made this choice** and what effect it has.
- It connects context to the **reader's response**, which is central to AO3.

activities.title: Quick check: matching context to text

question.text: Match each piece of historical context to the moment in the novella it helps to explain.
question.hint: Think about which characters or scenes show poverty, hard work, and attitudes to the poor.
question.explanation: Malthus's ideas are echoed in the 'surplus population' line. The Poor Law's workhouses appear in the charity collectors' scene. The low wages of clerks explain the Cratchits' poverty despite Bob having a job. The Ragged Schools movement relates to the child Ignorance, who represents uneducated poor children.

pairs.right: Scrooge says the poor should die to 'decrease the surplus population'
Scrooge asks the charity collectors whether the workhouses are still open

pairs.left: Low wages for clerks and labourers
pairs.right: The Cratchits struggle to afford a small goose even though Bob works full-time

pairs.left: The Ragged Schools movement for poor children
pairs.right: The Ghost of Christmas Present reveals the child called Ignorance

activities.title: Dickens's life and beliefs
activities.content:
## Why Dickens cared

Dickens was not writing about poverty from a comfortable distance. When he was twelve, his father was sent to a **debtors' prison** and Charles was taken out of school to work in a boot-blacking factory, sticking labels on jars for ten hours a day. He never forgot the shame and loneliness of it. Scrooge's lonely boyhood at school, and the neglected children he sees, carry echoes of this experience.

In 1843 Dickens visited a **Ragged School** in London, a free school for the poorest children, and was horrified by what he saw. He also read a government report on **child labour** in mines and factories. He planned to write an angry pamphlet, then decided a story would reach more people and hit harder. That story became *A Christmas Carol*.

## What Dickens believed

- **Education** was the key to breaking the cycle of poverty. That is why the ghost tells Scrooge to fear **Ignorance** even more than **Want**.
- **Christian charity** should be practical: feeding, warming and educating people, not just preaching at them.
- The rich had a **duty** to the poor because everyone is part of one society. Marley's ghost calls mankind Scrooge's *"business"*.

Dickens wanted to change hearts, and through hearts, to change how people acted.

question.text: Complete the sentences about Dickens's background.

metadata.blanksText: As a boy, Dickens was sent to work in a ___ factory after his father was imprisoned for ___. In 1843 he visited a ___ School for poor children, which helped inspire the novella.

question.hint: The factory made shoe polish; his father owed money; the schools were named after the children's torn clothes.
question.explanation: Dickens worked in a blacking (boot polish) factory after his father was jailed for debt. His visit to a Ragged School shocked him and fed into the figure of Ignorance.

activities.title: Christmas, Christianity and the carol form
activities.content:
## Reinventing Christmas

It is easy to assume Christmas has always been celebrated the way it is now. In fact, in the early 1800s many traditions had faded, especially in cities. Dickens's novella, along with new customs such as Christmas trees (popularised by Prince Albert) and Christmas cards (first sold in 1843), helped to build the modern festival of family, food and generosity.

For Dickens, Christmas was the one time of year when people opened their *"shut-up hearts"*, as Fred puts it in Stave One. He used the season as a lens: if people can be kind at Christmas, why not all year?

## Christianity

Victorian Britain was a strongly **Christian** society, and Dickens expected readers to recognise Christian ideas: forgiveness, redemption, charity and the warning that greed leads to damnation. Marley's chained ghost draws on traditional images of punishment after death. Scrooge's change is a **redemption**: a sinner saved by repentance. Tiny Tim's hope that people will *"remember upon Christmas Day, who made lame beggars walk"* points directly to the Gospels.

## Why a 'carol'?

A carol is a joyful song, often with a repeated refrain. Dickens divides his book into **staves** (verses) rather than chapters, and repeats ideas and phrases like a chorus. The form suggests the story is meant to be shared aloud and to bring people together, just as a carol does.

question.text: True or false: Dickens divided *A Christmas Carol* into 'staves' to make it resemble a piece of music with verses.
question.hint: Think about what the word 'carol' means and how songs are divided.
question.explanation: True. A stave is a verse of a song. By calling his chapters staves, Dickens links the book to the carol form: joyful, shared and repeated, with the message of goodwill acting like a chorus.

options.text: True
False

activities.title: How to use context well (AO3)
activities.content:
## Context that earns marks

AO3 asks you to show understanding of the **relationship** between a text and its context. The key word is *relationship*. A fact about Victorian Britain on its own scores nothing; a fact that **explains a choice Dickens made** scores well.

**Weak (bolt-on):**
> In Victorian times there were workhouses. Scrooge is mean to the poor.

**Strong (integrated):**
> Scrooge's casual question about whether the workhouses are "still in operation" reveals how the 1834 Poor Law allowed the wealthy to feel they had already done enough for the poor; Dickens uses this to show that cruelty can hide behind respectable systems.

**Useful sentence starters**
- *Dickens's original readers would have recognised…*
- *Writing in the Hungry Forties, Dickens…*
- *This reflects the Victorian belief that…*
- *Dickens challenges the common attitude that…*

**Three golden rules**
1. Keep context **brief** and **relevant**: one or two sentences, tied to a quotation.
2. Think about **purpose**: what did Dickens want his readers to feel or do?
3. Remember Dickens is often **arguing against** the attitudes of his time, not simply reflecting them.

question.text:
In Stave Three, the Ghost of Christmas Present shows Scrooge two children hidden in his robes and says: *"This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want. Beware them both... but most of all beware this boy."*

Explain how this moment reflects Dickens's views about Victorian society.
question.hint: Think about Dickens's belief in education, his visit to a Ragged School, and why ignorance might be more dangerous than hunger.
question.explanation: The children are allegories for the effects of poverty. Dickens believed education was the way out of poverty, so ignorance is the greater danger: uneducated children grow into adults who cannot escape, or who turn to crime, which threatens everyone. The moment reflects his shock at the Ragged Schools and his warning to wealthy readers that neglecting the poor will bring 'doom' to society as a whole.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the children are symbols or allegories of the effects of poverty on society
Links Ignorance to Dickens's belief in education or his visit to the Ragged Schools
Explains the warning to wealthy readers that neglecting the poor threatens the whole of society

question.text:
Read this short extract from Stave One, in which Scrooge replies to the gentlemen collecting for the poor.

> "If they would rather die," said Scrooge, "they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population. Besides—excuse me—I don't know that."

Starting with this extract, explain how Dickens uses Scrooge to criticise attitudes to poverty in Victorian society. Write about:

- how Dickens presents Scrooge's attitude in this extract
- how Dickens uses the rest of the novella to challenge such attitudes.
question.hint: Name the idea behind 'surplus population', explain how the ghost turns the phrase against Scrooge later, and think about the Cratchits, Ignorance and Want, and Scrooge's transformation.
question.explanation: A strong answer explains that 'surplus population' echoes Malthus and the harsh thinking behind the 1834 Poor Law; that 'I don't know that' shows wilful ignorance; that the Ghost of Christmas Present repeats the phrase about Tiny Tim to make the abstract personal; that the Cratchits show the working poor as loving and deserving; that Ignorance and Want warn of consequences; and that Scrooge's redemption models the change Dickens wanted in his readers.

markScheme.criterion: Links 'surplus population' to Malthus or to Victorian economic attitudes that excused neglect of the poor
Analyses Scrooge's language in the extract (e.g. 'I don't know that' as wilful ignorance, or the cold, business-like tone)
Refers to the Poor Law or workhouses as the context for Scrooge's views
Explains how the Ghost of Christmas Present repeats Scrooge's words to challenge him
Uses another relevant part of the novella (Cratchits, Ignorance and Want, Scrooge's transformation) to show Dickens challenging these attitudes
Comments on Dickens's purpose or the intended effect on his original readers

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Published **December 1843**, in the **Hungry Forties**, when industrial cities were full of poverty and disease.
- The **1834 Poor Law** forced the poor into harsh **workhouses**; Scrooge treats these as an adequate answer.
- **Malthus**'s idea of 'surplus population' is put in Scrooge's mouth so Dickens can expose it.
- Dickens's own **childhood** (blacking factory, father in debtors' prison) and his visit to a **Ragged School** shaped his belief in **education** and **practical charity**.
- **Christianity**, **redemption** and the joyful **carol form** (staves) frame the story.
- For AO3, tie context to a **quotation**, explain **Dickens's purpose**, and remember he often **challenges** the attitudes of his day.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in the best order for writing a paragraph that uses context effectively.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with a point and evidence; context should explain the evidence, not come first.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Make a point, support it with a quotation, analyse the language, then bring in context to explain why Dickens made that choice, and finish with the effect on readers.
order: Make a clear point about how Dickens presents an idea
Support the point with a short quotation
Analyse the language or method in the quotation
Bring in relevant context to explain Dickens's choice
Comment on the effect on Victorian and modern readers

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how the Cratchit family reflects the situation of the working poor in Victorian Britain, and what Dickens wants readers to feel about them.
practiceQuestions.hint: Bob has a job, yet the family cannot afford much. What does Dickens show about their character, and why?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bob works full-time as a clerk but earns so little that the family shares a small goose and Tiny Tim cannot get treatment. Dickens shows them as loving, grateful and dignified, so readers see the poor as deserving of sympathy and help rather than as lazy or 'surplus'.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that Bob works hard but low wages keep the family in poverty
Describes the family as loving, warm, grateful or dignified despite poverty
Explains Dickens's purpose: to make readers sympathise with the poor and reject the idea that they are lazy or undeserving

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best describes how Dickens uses Victorian context in the novella?
practiceQuestions.hint: Is Dickens agreeing with the common views of his time, or arguing against them?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dickens puts common Victorian attitudes into Scrooge's mouth and then shows them to be cruel and mistaken. He is challenging his society, not simply describing it.

options.text: He voices common Victorian attitudes through Scrooge in order to challenge and change them
He agrees with the Poor Law and wants readers to support workhouses
He avoids any reference to real social problems so the story feels timeless
He blames the poor for their own situation

practiceQuestions.text:
Read this short extract from Stave One, in which Marley's ghost speaks to Scrooge.

> "Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business."

How does Dickens use Marley's ghost to present ideas about social responsibility? Refer to the extract and to the Victorian context.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the repeated word 'business', the Christian idea of punishment, the chains made of cash-boxes, and what Dickens wanted wealthy readers to understand.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A good answer notes the repetition of 'business' redefining a commercial word to mean moral duty; the list of virtues as a Christian ideal; the chains as punishment for greed, drawing on religious imagery familiar to Victorian readers; Dickens's belief that the wealthy owed a duty to the poor in an industrial society; and his aim of persuading middle-class readers to act.

markScheme.criterion: Analyses the repetition of 'business' as redefining work or money-making as moral duty
Comments on the list of virtues (charity, mercy, etc.) as Christian or moral values
Refers to Marley's chains or punishment as a warning drawing on religious ideas of the afterlife
Links to the Victorian context of wealth and poverty, the Poor Law or the idea that the rich had a duty to the poor
Explains Dickens's purpose or the intended effect on readers

practiceQuestions.hint: Scrooge asks whether they are 'still in operation' and thinks the poor should go there.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Workhouses were institutions where the destitute received basic food and shelter in return for hard, monotonous labour under harsh conditions. Families were separated, and many people would rather die than enter one.

options.text: An institution where the destitute were given basic food and shelter in return for hard labour under harsh conditions
A factory where children were paid to make shoe polish
options.feedback: That describes the blacking factory where Dickens worked as a boy.

options.text: A free school for poor children run by volunteers
A prison for people who had committed violent crimes

practiceQuestions.text: Match each piece of Victorian context to the feature of the novella it helps to explain.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about ghost stories at Christmas, Dickens's father, a way of thinking that counted everything, and the new fashion for family Christmas.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The novella is a Christmas ghost story in the Victorian tradition. Dickens's father's time in a debtors' prison explains his sympathy for the couple who owe money to the dead man. Utilitarian thinking, obsessed with facts and figures, is reflected in Scrooge's ledgers and cash-boxes. The Victorian revival of Christmas as a family festival is reflected in Fred's games and the Cratchits' dinner.

pairs.right: The whole novella is framed as a supernatural tale set on Christmas Eve

pairs.right: Dickens's sympathy for the young couple relieved by their creditor's death

pairs.left: Utilitarian thinking that valued facts and figures above feelings
pairs.right: Scrooge's obsession with ledgers, accounts and cash-boxes

pairs.left: The revival of Christmas as a family festival in the 1840s
pairs.right: Fred's party games and the Cratchits' Christmas dinner

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about Dickens and his times.

metadata.blanksText: Dickens wrote *A Christmas Carol* in only about ___ weeks in the autumn of 1843. As a child he was deeply affected when his father was sent to the ___ debtors' prison. The economist Thomas ___ argued that population would grow faster than the food supply.

practiceQuestions.hint: The book was written very quickly; the prison in Southwark shares its name with a famous later novel's setting; the economist's name lies behind 'surplus population'.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dickens wrote the novella in about six weeks. His father was imprisoned in the Marshalsea. Thomas Malthus's population theory lies behind Scrooge's phrase about the surplus population.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: in 1843 there was no state pension, unemployment benefit or free healthcare, so the poor depended on private charity or the workhouse.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about why the charity collectors are going from door to door.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. The welfare state did not exist. Apart from the workhouse, the poor relied on charity, which is why Dickens stresses the duty of the wealthy to give.

options.text: True
False
options.feedback: State welfare did not exist; charity and the workhouse were the only safety nets.

practiceQuestions.text: In Stave Four, the Spirit shows Scrooge a young couple who are relieved, even joyful, to learn that the man they owed money to has died. Explain how this moment reflects Dickens's views about Victorian society.
practiceQuestions.hint: Who is the dead creditor? Think about Dickens's own family history with debt, and about what it means when a death brings only relief.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The dead creditor is Scrooge himself, shown as so merciless that his death brings a struggling family relief rather than grief. Dickens, whose father was imprisoned for debt, knew how the fear of creditors crushed ordinary people. The moment warns wealthy readers that a life spent squeezing money out of others leaves no one to mourn, and urges mercy and kindness in place of hard business.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the dead man is Scrooge, a harsh creditor whose death brings relief rather than grief
Links to the context of debt (debtors' prisons, the Marshalsea, Dickens's father, poverty)
Explains the warning to wealthy readers that money without kindness leaves nobody to mourn, and the call for mercy

practiceQuestions.text:
Starting with this moment from Stave Four, explain how Dickens uses reactions to Scrooge's death to criticise attitudes to money and community in Victorian society.

*Scrooge watches a group of businessmen discuss the death of a man whose name is not given. One says he thought the man would never die; another asks only what he has done with his money. They joke that it will be a very cheap funeral because nobody will attend, and one adds that he will go only "if a lunch is provided".*

Write about:

- how Dickens presents the businessmen's attitude in this moment
- how Dickens uses the rest of the novella to challenge such attitudes.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look at the joke about the cheap funeral and the question about money. Notice that Scrooge does not yet realise it is his own death. Then use Marley's chain, Old Joe's, Belle or Stave Five to show what Dickens wants readers to learn.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the businessmen show indifference and self-interest: their only questions concern money and lunch, and their casual joke about a cheap funeral treats a death as a business item. The dramatic irony that Scrooge cannot see it is himself lets the reader judge before he does. Dickens links this to a Victorian business culture that measured people by wealth, and challenges it through Marley's chain of cash-boxes, the thieves at Old Joe's, Belle's warning about the golden idol, and Scrooge's reversal in Stave Five, when he rejoins the community. His purpose is to warn readers that money without human connection ends in a lonely, unmourned death.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the businessmen's indifference or callous humour towards the death
Analyses the language: 'cheap funeral', the focus on money, or 'lunch is provided' as self-interest
Comments on the dramatic irony that Scrooge does not realise the dead man is himself while the reader does
Links to Victorian context (business or utilitarian values, a society that measured people by wealth)
Uses another part of the novella to show the consequences of greed or isolation (Marley's chain, Old Joe's, Belle, Stave Five)
Comments on Dickens's purpose or the intended effect on readers
